children: By Krystal Hu

It's a hectic week here at Reuters: My intrepid colleague Echo Wang got to see Anthropic's confidential IPO prospectus before anyone else did. It's the clearest look yet inside the financials and vision of one of the largest IPOs in the world — the document every investor and competitor has been dying to see. You can read her scoop here.

Our team combed through more than 300 pages to pull out what actually matters. One thing that caught my attention: how often the Big Tech giants show up in this filing — as distribution partners, financial backers, computer suppliers, and competitors, all at once. We've got the clearest view yet of how circular this AI world really is, and how much a lab's success depends on the giants it's also competing against. Anthropic has not commented on the filing.

For the first time, we were able to calculate that Anthropic pays to Big Tech roughly 16% of every dollar it earns through cloud partners. It counts the full value of contracts sold through a cloud marketplace as revenue, then treats the platform's cut as a marketing cost. OpenAI does the opposite by only counting what it keeps after the cloud partner takes its share. That difference matters for understanding the big numbers floating around, and how to actually compare the two rivals' toplines as they both eye the public market.
There's much more. Scroll down for my Q&A with Echo, where she walks me through what surprised her most, and what she's hearing from her sources about the IPO.

INSIDE ANTHROPIC’S IPO FILING: A Q&A WITH THE REPORTER WHO BROKE THE STORY

Echo Wang is the Reuters editor in charge of the US M&A team. She also covers IPOs for us, breaking the news on not one but possibly two of the largest ever IPOs — first SpaceX, now the upcoming Anthropic. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
K: Echo, you did it again. How is this time different from when you got the SpaceX filing in the summer?

Echo: SpaceX was our first real encounter with a trillion-dollar IPO. Even people who had worked on enormous deals were seeing things they hadn’t seen before. The company had an unusual amount of say over the process, and, as a reporter, it felt like every day brought another surprise.
Anthropic shares that level of control, but the information lockdown feels tighter still. Sources have described it as the strictest they’ve encountered. Still, we managed to do our work.
K: Did the filing change your understanding of Anthropic the way SpaceX’s changed your understanding of SpaceX?

Echo: Not in quite the same way. Early in our SpaceX coverage, a lot of people thought of Starlink as the crown jewel: a profitable connectivity business with a trajectory investors could understand. By the time we saw the company prospectus, the bigger story was that SpaceX had become an AI business. That was a remarkable shift to watch over a few months.

With Anthropic, people already know they’re looking at a leading AI company, particularly in enterprise AI. The surprises are less about what kind of company this is and more about the numbers that had been kept private — its margins and losses.
K: What stood out in Anthropic’s financials?

Echo: The $42 billion net loss, even knowing that roughly $34 billion of it came from financing write-downs, which leaves the operating loss a little over $8 billion. I understand the argument for valuing a fast-growing technology company on what it might earn in a few years. Investors and advisers we spoke with were looking at projected revenue for 2027 and 2028. But seeing those losses alongside talk of a potential $2 trillion IPO valuation — it’s one thing to understand the logic in the abstract and another to see the figures on the page.
K: You noticed a contrast in how SpaceX and Anthropic talk about the future. Walk us through it.
Echo: Yes. Reading the two filings, that really struck me. Risk factors took up about a third of Anthropic’s roughly 300-page filing, compared with around 30 pages in SpaceX’s filing.

These could be two of the largest IPOs in history, only months apart, and both are bound up with AI. Yet one filing leans so heavily into the promise of the future, while the other asks investors to consider the possibility of ending it. I find that a profound contrast. SpaceX presents this sweeping aspiration for humanity: going to Mars, becoming a spacefaring civilization. Anthropic talks about what AI could make possible, but it also confronts what could go terribly wrong. Its filing warns that AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
K: What did you learn about who would control Anthropic as a public company?

Echo: The filing describes a “Founder LLC” involving Anthropic’s seven co-founders. Through Class F shares, they would collectively hold 50.1% of the voting power on corporate matters, including board elections.

A founder retaining control after an IPO isn’t unusual in tech. What caught my attention was the collective control through this vehicle, with the seven co-founders exercising control together. Palantir has a comparable founder-control arrangement, though the structures aren’t identical. It’s a detail worth paying attention to when you’re asking who ultimately gets to steer the company.
K: Is Anthropic still a 2026 IPO?

Echo: I wish I had a crystal ball. The public filing had been expected by the end of September, and a roadshow around mid-October; those plans appear to have slipped, as we reported earlier. Some people have begun thinking it could happen after the midterm elections. We’re still reporting on the development of the specific timeframe.

The broader IPO market has become less welcoming, and there are questions particular to AI as well. A few months ago, investors seemed more certain about Anthropic’s position as the enterprise AI leader. Many still see it as a leader, but the picture appears less straightforward now. When that happens, people take more time to think through a bet of this size.
